    for rank in range(size):

🚀 Feature

Allow torch.diagflat to create sparse tensors.
Motivation

torch.diagflat will return a Tensor that is sparse, but stored as a dense Tensor.
It takes up a large amount of memory just to store, and for most use cases of creating a diagonal matrix, it will stay mainly diagonal.
Having the option of creating the sparse Tensor should speed up computation for large Tensors, whilst not breaking existing code. In my research, this has led to some CUDA out of memory errors that torch.sparse_coo_tensor avoided.
Pitch

Change torch.diagflat function signature to:
 torch.diagflat(input, offset=0, sparse=False) → Tensor
This argument name could be layout for consistency with the sparse docs, but I think this would be confusing as you might think you're declaring row/column-major here instead.
Alternatives

Create dense Tensor and make sparse, i.e. torch.diagflat(input).to_sparse() which may lead to out of memory errors
Create Tensor individually by values via generators in torch.sparse_coo_tensor` which is less practical, e.g.:

>>> x = torch.arange(5)
>>> torch.sparse_coo_tensor(torch.tensor([(i, i) for i in range(len(x))]).T, x)
cc: #9674
cc @aocsa @nikitaved @pearu @mruberry
nodes.title: Sparse return type for `torch.diagflat`

Today in PyTorch we have TORCH_WARN and TORCH_WARN_ONCE. TORCH_WARN_ONCE, as its name suggests, only throws a warning one time. This makes it tricky to test for. Our test suite, for example, has maybeWarnsRegex, but this just verifies that no other warnings are thrown.

🐛 Bug
Grad on torch.symeig gives the wrong value if there are repeated eigenvalues (degeneracy exists), even though the grad should be finite.
To Reproduce
import torch
torch.manual_seed(126)
n = 5
kwargs = {
    "dtype": torch.float64,
}
# random matrix to be orthogonalized for the eigenvectors
mat = torch.randn((n, n), **kwargs).requires_grad_()

# matrix for the loss function
P2 = torch.randn((n, n), **kwargs).requires_grad_()

# the degenerate eigenvalues
a = torch.tensor([0.5, 1.0, 2.0], **kwargs).requires_grad_()

def get_loss(a, mat, P2):
    # get the orthogonal vector for the eigenvectors
    P, _ = torch.qr(mat)

    # line up the eigenvalues
    b = torch.cat((a[:2], a[1:2], a[2:], a[2:]))

    # construct the matrix
    diag = torch.diag_embed(b)
    A = torch.matmul(torch.matmul(P.T, diag), P)

    U = eivecs[:, 1:3]  # the degenerate eigenvectors

🐛 Bug
When torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR is used in a specific way (where the optimizer and the scheduler are both attached to an object instance and the lambda function refers to an instance variable), a GPU memory leak is observed.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
Run the following code to reproduce the behavior.
import torch


weight = torch.nn.Linear(100, 100).to("cuda")


class Foo:
    def __init__(self):
        self.lr = 1.0
        self.op = torch.optim.Adam(weight.parameters())
        self.sc = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(self.op, lr_lambda=lambda s: self.lr)

    def run(self):
        loss = weight(torch.randn(32, 100).to("cuda")).mean()
        self.op.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        self.sc.step()
        self.op.step()


while True:
    Foo().run()
A gradual increase in peak memory usage is observed in the main GPU device. This will cause OOM error eventually.
Note: The reason why the LR scheduler is allocated for each loop is I need to run the same code multiple times in a single process. The above snippet is just a barebone structure of the problematic code.
Expected behavior
The memory leak should not happen. For contrasting examples, the following code examples do not exhibit memory leaks.

The LR scheduler does not make a reference to any instance-specific variables.

weight = torch.nn.Linear(100, 100).to("cuda")


class Foo:
    def __init__(self):
        self.lr = 1.0
        self.op = torch.optim.Adam(weight.parameters())
        self.sc = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(self.op, lr_lambda=lambda s: 1.0)  # no reference to the instance field

        self.op.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        self.sc.step()
        self.op.step()


while True:
    Foo().run()

weight = torch.nn.Linear(100, 100).to("cuda")


while True:

🚀 Feature: Return the attention scores from all heads
Return the attention scores from all heads in the MultiHeadAttention Module and multi_head_attention_forward. The current implementation only allows returning the averaged attention score over all heads
In short: add option to change

  
    
      pytorch/torch/nn/functional.py
    
    
         Line 4309
      in
      16c72a5
    
  
  
    

        
          
           return attn_output, attn_output_weights.sum(dim=1) / num_heads 
        
    
  


into
return attn_output, attn_output_weights
Motivation
The motivating idea behind Multi-Head attention is to perform the attention mechanism in parallel and allow the model to attend to different sequence elements with each head separately. The current torch code (MultiHeadAttention Module and multi_head_attention_forward) allows to return the attn_output_weights along with the attn_output.
However, the attn_output_weights are averaged over all heads.  The attention scores for each separate head are not accessible to the outside.
Why should it be possible to get attention scores for each head?

Each head attends to different sequence elements. The information to which sequence elements each head attends to is lost when attention scores are averaged over all heads. The attention scores for each head are important to understand the features that are extracted in each layer (touches: feature importance, explainability).
This averaging behavior in attn_output_weights is inconsistent with attn_output where the embedding dimensions are grouped into head_dim blocks from the same attention head.

  
    
      pytorch/torch/nn/functional.py
    
    
         Line 4124
      in
      16c72a5
    
  
  
    

        
          
           head_dim = embed_dim // num_heads 
        
    
  



Pitch
I would propose

modifying the need_weights=True option in multi_head_attention_forward to a choice [all, average, none] to control the return behavior of multi_head_attention_forward. The option need_weights=avg would be equivalent to current need_weights=True and need_weights=all would return attn_output_weights without summation and average with num_heads here. Alternatives like changing the current behavior or adding a second boolean need_all_weights flag are possible too.
carrying the need_weights option to the MultiHeadAttention Module to make it easily accessible to the outside when using the MultiHeadAttention module.

I am happy to write a pull request with the modifications in multi_head_attention_forward and MultiHeadAttention Module according to further discussion or to leave the concrete implementation choices to the maintainers.
Overall, it would be great to have this option in the PyTorch code. This would make the code mode cleaner and would allow understanding the different head behaviors without having to locally modify the pytorch functions.
Alternatives
Current alternatives are:

creating multiple MultiHeadAttention modules hardcoded with a single head to retrieve the attention scores of this head (probably less efficient)
copying and modifying the multi_head_attention_forward function and MultiHeadAttention Module locally.

cc @albanD @mruberry @zhangguanheng66

def worker(rank):

    dist.init_process_group(backend='nccl', world_size=NUM_GPUS, rank=rank)

    def parallelize(module):

    # all workers have the same initial model

🚀 Feature
For the pytorch operator torch.split(tensor, split_size_or_sections, dim) we would like the input split_size_or_sections to also handle tensors. Right now it handles list of ints and an int.
Motivation
When tracing a model, we currently do split_size_or_sections=tensor.tolist() when calling torch.split but tracing can't record this conversion of tensor to list of ints so the traced model fails on other inputs. This is currently blocking a diff that tries to improve runtime performance by using tensor operations, D24595761.
Pitch
Have torch.split(tensor, tensor, int) work so that tracing can properly record the operations for a traced model.
Alternatives
We currently don't have alternatives (I think). We are migrating to a scripted model (which works in this case) but support for tracing is still requested.
Additional context
Here is a diff D24595761 that tries to improve performance by using torch operators only but fails for a traced model

🚀 Feature
To give user more information about python level functions in profiler traces, we propose to add some instrumenting on the following functions:

_BaseDataLoaderIter.__next__
Optimizer.step
Optimizer.zero_grad

Motivation
Current profiler mainly focus on C++ level operators. It lacks profiling on python side functions, such as dataloading, optimizer, module.forward, tensor.backward, and so on.
We did some user study and get this requirement.
The related issue: #45629
Pitch
We propose to instrument the 3 functions listed in "Feature".
We add the next code at the head of each function body to profile it:
with torch.autograd.profiler.record_function("<name>")
The "<name>" is in pattern "<Type>#<Class>.<Method>". Text of <Type> is both for user easy to understand and for profiler uniquely identify its kind, it is not restricted to real code.
For example, "enumerate(DataLoader)#_SingleProcessDataLoaderIter.__next__", Optimizer.step#SGD.step, Optimizer.zero_grad#SGD.zero_grad
For Optimizer.step, because it is only called into inherited class, in order to avoid instrument every inherited class’s “step”, we assign a wrapper function to the self.step in Optimizer.__init__. Then the wrapper function will be called by every inherited class. In the wrapper, we call self.step under the record_function context manager.
Alternatives
As discussed with @ilia-cher, using decorator or __getattribute__ to instrument is bad style so we drop it.
Additional context
We've talked with @ilia-cher, @gdankel and reach an initial agreement on it.
PR #47655

🚀 Feature

Currently, we are using the ascii variant of the Windows API. But apparently it is problematic when user passes in non-ascii strings in fields like filenames, paths and etc. It has caused problems like pytorch/vision#2931.
The usages of Windows API exist in those sources:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/csrc/jit/codegen/fuser/cpu/temp_file.h
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/csrc/jit/codegen/fuser/cpu/fused_kernel.cpp
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/TH/THAllocator.cpp
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/c10/util/Backtrace.cpp

Details
There are mainly two ways that users could pass in a string to our core library, including

from PyTorch through pybind11

In this case, if we use std::string or const char* as the argument type, it will convert the string to utf-8 automatically. But unluckily, Windows API don't accept UTF-8 strings.

from LibTorch

In this case, if we use std::string or const char* as the argument type, the string will be encoded according to the user's locale. (e.g. for Chinese users, it will be using GB2312. ) It stills need to the conversion to UTF-16 btw.
Options
We have two options here.

Convert it to UTF-16 and call the unicode variant of the Windows API. This is easy to implement. But the difficulty lies in the problem that how we tell whether a string is encoded by utf-8, ascii or anything else? (Or maybe we just claim that we only accepts utf-8 strings?) (An alternative is the /utf-8 switch. We could mark it as public argument for CMake. https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/build/reference/utf-8-set-source-and-executable-character-sets-to-utf-8?view=msvc-150)
Use std::wstring as string argument type. It avoids the conversion, but we will have to redesign all of our APIs. What' s more, It's hard to maintain. Because conventionally, we should implement both the unicode version and the ascii version and select them through the existence of the _UNICODE macro.

#ifdef _UNICODE
#define test test_unicode
#else

We have a CenterNet implementation traced as a TorchScript model and saved as both in a quantized and unquantized variant.
One of the results our CenterNet modle produces is a heatmap that contains for every pixel a score corresponding to the likelihood of the pixel being the center of an object visible in the input image.
A decent example of such a centerpoint heatmap could look like this:


When we run the forward pass in different Android Apps directly via the Java bindings, both variants produces decent results as the one seen above.
When we run the forward pass via the C++ front-end directly on a Ubuntu 18.04 docker container on our x86 PCs both variants produces decent results as the one seen above
When we run the forward pass on Android Apps via binding a C++ frontend into the app through NDK and JNI-calls , we see that the unquantized model gives the decent result we expect, but the quantized model produces a centerpoint heatmap with clear artifacts. An example can be seen below:


As you can see it shows a very particular pattern that is consistently produced on every run in different apps while capturing different scenery.
We also used both a pre-compiled version of libtorch following this tutorial https://pytorch.org/tutorials/recipes/android_native_app_with_custom_op.html
